Frequently asked questions

Source: vignettes/faq.Rmd
faq.Rmd

Data

How do I bring my own data in?

mt_data() takes long data frames, one row per cell, with a column for deaths, exposures or population and columns for age, period and strata. Ages can be single years, labels such as "<1", "01-04", "85-89", "90+", "85 and over", or two columns with lower and upper bounds:

parse_age_labels(c("<1", "01-04", "85-89", "90+", "85 and over"))
#>          label age_lo age_hi
#>         <char>  <num>  <num>
#> 1:          <1      0      1
#> 2:       01-04      1      5
#> 3:       85-89     85     90
#> 4:         90+     90    Inf
#> 5: 85 and over     85    Inf
d <- data.frame(region = "A", year = 2019, age = c("85-89", "90+"), deaths = c(120, 210),
                exposure = c(2500, 1400))
mt_data(deaths = d, exposure = d, by = "region")
#> <mt_data> 1 stratum by region, omega = 110
#>   deaths     5-year groups 85-89, 90+; periods 2019-2019 (width 1); 2 cells
#>   exposure   5-year groups 85-89, 90+; periods 2019-2019 (width 1); 2 cells
#>   grid       <mt_axis: age, 2 intervals> 85-89 90+
#>              <mt_axis: period, 1 interval> 2019

Deaths and exposures may come at different resolutions (for example deaths in 5-year groups, exposures by single year of age). Tables in wide format, with one value column per sex or cause, are read by listing the columns (value = list(deaths = c(female = "Female", male = "Male"))). Values given as text with symbols for suppressed or missing cells (".", "x", "-") are recognised; other symbols are declared with missing and zero. Readers exist for Human Mortality Database tables (mt_from_hmd(), mt_read_hmd()), GENESIS and GBE-Bund exports from Destatis (mt_read_genesis(), mt_read_gbe()), StMoMoData and demogdata objects (as_mt_data()).

I have populations on 31 December, not exposures. What now?

Read them as population and convert them with mt_as_exposure(), whose type says what the counts are: "dec31" for populations on 31 December (the exposure of year t is the mean of the populations on 31 December of t - 1 and t), "jan1" for populations on 1 January, "midyear" for mid-year estimates. Exposures are the denominator of the rates, so this choice matters for the level of every forecast.

What does mt_validate() check?

Cells with zero exposure, deaths without exposure, death rates above one below age 100, missing values, strata without deaths or exposures, levels that look like totals of other levels (for example "Insgesamt" among the regions), grid cells without observations, and, with a hierarchy, whether totals equal the sums of their parts (deaths and exposures add up over regions or sexes; rates add up over causes, mt_hierarchy(cause = list(total = "all", additive = "rates"))).

Granularity and ungrouping

Should I model single years of age or the age groups of my data?

Model at the resolution the question needs. Life expectancy, probabilities of dying and age-standardised rates can be computed from 5-year groups (the life table uses the interval widths). Single years are needed when results are reported by single year, when a model needs them (cohort models such as APC need equal age and period steps), or when data at different resolutions are combined. Backtests always score against the deaths at their observed resolution, so ungrouping errors count against the model, and mt_backtest() with and without step_ungroup() answers the question for your data.

Which ungrouping method should I use?

The penalized composite link model (mt_ungroup(), default) ungroups deaths as rates with the exposures as offset and keeps group totals exactly. On England & Wales data grouped into 5-year groups, it and the spline methods ("hyman_kannisto", "natural_gompertz", "gam") were almost as close to the known single years as the Poisson noise allows; they differed in the last, wide age group, where the PCLM was closest. Check your own result with mt_plot_ungroup() and mt_ungroup_check(); see “Ungrouping age groups: methods and diagnostics”.

Can I split the open interval 90+ into single years?

Only from assumptions: the data say nothing about the age pattern inside the interval. mt_ungroup() warns when it extrapolates. Prefer a grid whose open interval starts where the data’s does, or data with a higher open age (for example exposures to 100+ with deaths to 90+, where the exposures carry the age pattern).

Models and uncertainty

Which model should I use?

There is no single best model; a rolling-origin backtest on your own data (mt_backtest(), horizons like the ones you will report) decides. As a starting point:

Situation Try first Why
One population, many deaths per cell, single years or 5-year groups lee_carter(), rwd() and ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), rw = rwd()) Lee-Carter is the standard; single models give too narrow intervals on real data, the ensemble is better calibrated
Several strata that should not diverge (sexes, regions, deprivation groups) li_lee(common_by = ...) a common trend with bounded deviations; pools information across strata
Small populations, many cells with few deaths li_lee(common_by = ...), wider age groups (mt_regroup()), step_smooth(); rwd(observation_noise = TRUE) in ensembles pooling and smoothing reduce noise; the plain random walk accumulates it
Totals and parts must add up reconciled(model, hierarchy) bottom-up for joint models, WLS for separate models
Causes of death separate or Li-Lee models per cause, reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up") with cause = list(total = "all", additive = "rates") cause rates add up to the all-cause rate
Cohort effects (for example generations born around 1925-1945) apc_bayes(), stmomo("apc") age-period models attribute cohort patterns to period trends
Trend change in the recent past step_window(years) with a backtest of several windows a shorter fitting period follows the recent trend

Check every fit with summary(fit), mt_parameters(fit) and mt_plot_residuals(fit), and every forecast for warnings about implausible rates.

Why are my 95% intervals too narrow (or too wide)?

Intervals of most models describe the uncertainty of their own assumptions, for example a constant drift. On real data, changes of trend add uncertainty that these assumptions leave out, so intervals tend to be too narrow over 5 to 10 years: in backtests on HMD and ONS data the 95% coverage of Lee-Carter was 0.70 to 0.84. The plain random walk is wider, because year-to-year changes of observed rates contain observation noise twice; that extra width happened to give good 95% coverage on real data. rwd(observation_noise = TRUE) removes the double counting and is sharper (lower CRPS), with intervals that were too narrow on real data. Mixtures of models (ensemble()) widen the intervals where the models disagree. recalibrated() rescales the spread of any model’s draws to its forecast errors in the last years of the training data (by default ten); on England & Wales men it raised the 95% coverage of Lee-Carter from 0.75 to 0.88. Check calibration with mt_backtest() and mt_plot_coverage().

How do I choose smoothing and model parameters by forecast accuracy?

This is tuning: fit each candidate setting to the years up to T - h, forecast the last h years, and keep the setting that forecast them best, then refit it to all years. mt_tune() does this for any grid of settings, including preprocessing, and tuned() makes it part of a model, so that an outer backtest repeats the choice at each origin without seeing the test years:

grid <- expand.grid(k = c(10, 30), order = 1:6)
spec <- tuned(function(order, k) hyndman_ullah(order = order, smooth_args = list(k = k)), grid,
              inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 10, metric = "rmse")

inner_origins = 1 is a single hold-out of the last ten years; several origins (inner_origins = 3, inner_h = 5) average over more periods. metric = "rmse" chooses by point accuracy, "crps" by the whole forecast distribution, and target = "life_expectancy" by the quantity of interest. recalibrated() answers a different question: it keeps the model and rescales the width of its intervals to the recent forecast errors. The two combine as recalibrated(tuned(...)).

Should I smooth the data before forecasting?

Smoothing over age can help where cells hold few deaths (rare causes, small regions); check it in a backtest, as the applied vignettes do. Smoothing over time removes the year-to-year noise from the fitted trends and from the start of the forecast, but also the variation from which models such as Lee-Carter estimate the uncertainty of their period index: alone, it made intervals too narrow in backtests (95% coverage of Lee-Carter 0.59 instead of 0.75 on England & Wales men). Most of the gain there comes from recalibrated(), which re-estimates the spread against the raw observations: calibration alone gave a CRPS of 0.0657 and a coverage of 0.88 (against 0.0687 and 0.75); Whittaker smoothing over time added nothing to it, the age-period GAM a little (0.0646, coverage 0.91). On the ONS quintiles smoothing over time made the forecasts worse (“Smoothing death rates”). Treat it as optional and check it in a backtest. Use smoothing as a preprocessing step (mt_prep(step_smooth(...))), never on the data before fitting (mt_backtest() stops, mt_fit() warns), so that backtests refit it on each training window and models take their observation noise from the raw rates. mt_smooth_check() and mt_plot_smooth() show what the smoothing removed.

Why does the forecast start with a step?

Most models start from their fitted rates of the last observed year. When the fit misses the level of the last years, the first forecast year jumps away from the observations; mt_jump_off() reports the step, and the forecast plots show it as a gap between the solid (fitted) and the dashed (forecast) line. anchored(model, years = 3) moves the start to the observed level of the last three years, fading out over ten years (so forecasts more than ten years ahead are those of the model); it improved short-term accuracy on England & Wales men and on the ONS data. Starting from the observed rates of the last year alone (lee_carter(jump_off = "observed"), or anchored(years = 1, decay = Inf, shrink = FALSE)) was best on England & Wales men (CRPS 0.0583 against 0.0639 anchored to three years), whose counts are large, and worse on the ONS quintiles, whose last year is noisier. Decompositions of a change from an observed to a forecast year include the step; mt_decompose() reports it (jump_off) and can start from the fitted rates (observed = "fitted").

What is the difference between predictive draws and forecast rates?

For models of smooth rates (Lee-Carter, Li-Lee, Tucker3, FDM, StMoMo, Bayesian APC, rwd(observation_noise = TRUE)), mt_forecast() returns draws of the smooth death rates by default, and predictive = TRUE adds the variation of observed rates around them (extra-Poisson and Poisson noise given the exposures), which is what an observed future rate will show. Models of observed rates (rwd(), arima_series(), ets_series()) forecast observed rates directly, and predictive adds nothing. Backtests use predictive draws because they are compared with observed rates. For life expectancy and other summaries of the underlying mortality, use the default draws.

How do I handle small populations and zero deaths?

Models that take logs of observed rates (the random walk, the SVD version of Lee-Carter, Li-Lee) replace zero deaths by 0.5, which is harmless for a few cells and distorting for many. The Poisson Lee-Carter gives age groups without any death a constant rate and shrinks the age pattern of change where the counts are too sparse, with a warning. With many small cells:

  • model at a coarser resolution (age groups instead of single years, or wider groups at young ages, mt_regroup());
  • pool information across strata, for example li_lee(common_by = "sex") for regions or deprivation groups, or borrow strength across ages and years within a stratum with the smoothing priors of apc_bayes();
  • smooth before fitting with step_smooth() (age 0 is left out by default);
  • use rwd(observation_noise = TRUE) instead of rwd(), alone or in an ensemble: the plain random walk treats the Poisson noise of observed rates as real change, and its paths over 10 or more years can reach impossible rates;
  • combine rare causes of death into larger groups (see ons_cause_groups and mt_group_levels()).

mt_forecast() warns when forecast death rates exceed 1, the clearest sign that a model is unstable for the data.

Which function aggregates what?

Function Combines Example
mt_regroup() ages or periods single years to 5-year groups, or to the groups of another table
mt_group_levels() levels of one stratum variable, replacing them deciles to quintiles, causes to cause groups
mt_aggregate_strata() strata along a hierarchy, adding totals and groups as new strata regions to East, West and Germany, sexes to both sexes
mt_aggregate_draws() forecast draws along a hierarchy or to wider age groups forecasts for Germany from forecasts by Land

How should I treat the COVID-19 years?

Either end the training data in 2019 (as in the ONS vignettes), or mark the years as shocks so that the trend is estimated without them:

prep <- mt_prep(step_shocks(2020:2022, action = "interpolate"))
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), data, prep = prep)

Whether mortality returns to the pre-pandemic trend is an assumption the model does not test.

Coherence

How do I get forecasts that add up over regions, sexes or causes?

Describe the structure with mt_hierarchy() and either model the bottom strata and sum them (reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up")), or model every node and reconcile the draws (method = "wls", "mint", …). Totals that are not in the data are added by mt_aggregate_strata(). To keep a trusted total, such as an all-cause forecast that the causes must add up to, give it as fixed and use method = "proportional" (its parts are scaled in proportion to their forecasts) or "wls" (the most uncertain parts absorb the difference). Over long horizons, sums of cause forecasts tend to be more pessimistic than forecasts of all causes (Wilmoth 1995), so compare the two before choosing. Reconciliation of deaths uses exposures of the forecast years; supply population projections as exposure when they are available. See “Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts” and the applied vignettes “Inequality in England” and “Differences between the German Laender”.

Will the gap between regions or deprivation groups keep growing?

That depends on the model, not only on the data. Separate models per stratum extrapolate each stratum’s trend, so gaps can widen without bound. li_lee() and product_ratio() let strata deviate from a common trend only through stationary processes, so gaps return towards their past average. Backtests over a few years rarely separate the two; the choice is an assumption to state.

Which ages and causes explain a gap, and how much is composition?

mt_decompose() splits a difference in life expectancy (or in the probability of dying, an age-standardised or crude rate, or any function of the rates) into contributions of ages and causes: between strata in one year (var, ref), between years (periods, which may combine an observed and a forecast year), or between two forecasts (y). With groups, it also separates the composition of a population of subgroups from the change of their mortality: for groups defined at birth or for life, such as sex or education, as in Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024) (composition = "radix"); for areas such as deprivation quintiles, whose populations move between groups, with composition = "pooled". Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so contributions have intervals; see “Decomposing differences in life expectancy”.

Practicalities

Are forecasts reproducible?

Yes, with a seed (mt_forecast(..., seed = 1), mt_backtest(..., seed = 1)). Backtests and recalibrated() seed every origin separately, so their results do not depend on cores. Fits of several strata in parallel (mt_fit(..., cores = )) run in forked processes; for models with random steps in the fit, set RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG") and a seed before the call to make them reproducible.

How long does it take?

Lee-Carter, Li-Lee and random walks fit in seconds even for hundreds of strata. One-dimensional PCLM ungrouping takes about two seconds per stratum for 30 years of single ages; the two-dimensional version is much slower. apc_bayes() runs MCMC chains: with mcmc_control("fast") from about ten seconds (8 age groups, 10 years) to one or two minutes per stratum (19 age groups, 14 years).

Where do the validation numbers come from?

The validation/ directory of the source repository runs benchmarks with thresholds on every change (ungrouping accuracy, interval calibration, coherence). The vignette “Comparison with demography, bamp and StMoMo” reports accuracy and interval coverage of the models on four data sets.

References

Wilmoth JR (1995). Are mortality projections always more pessimistic when disaggregated by cause of death? Mathematical Population Studies 5(4): 293-319. doi:10.1080/08898489509525409.
